newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel, Tietmeyer reach agreement on reserves.
newsitem.headline: Waigel, Tietmeyer reach agreement on reserves.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said on Thursday they have reached an agreement on revaluing the central bank's currency reserves.
The central bank will use room provided by the Maastricht treaty to revalue its foreign exchange reserves in 1997 using accounting rules provided for in existing law.
"These make it possible to carry out a valuation close to market prices and retain the principle of lowest value," the statement said.
The statement said that the Finance Ministry and the Bundesbank had reached an agreement affecting foreign exchange reserves but made no mention of gold reserves.

The statement made clear that with the beginning of the third phase of monetary union, the central bank will be able to use accounting practices that have been created for the planned European central bank.
"The Bundesbank intends to make use of this possibility," the statement said.
Economists believe the central bank will use the lowest annual exchange rate in revaluing its foreign exchange reserves, which would still be higher than current book rates.

Sources close to the Bundesbank have indicated the central bank might be willing to revalue its dollar reserves to between 1.50-1.55 marks, up from current book rate of 1.36 marks, but still well below the current market exchange rate.
The revaluation would affect the balance sheet of the central bank for 1997 and the finance ministry said profits from the transaction would be transferred to the federal government in 1998.
The statement added that the Bundesbank would be consulted in the event that any changes were necessary to the law regulating the central bank's activities.
Waigel and Tietmeyer appear satisfied with the result of the meeting in the Bonn finance ministry.
"We have not only found a solution, but I think it is a good and sturdy solution," Tietmeyer said.

The meeting on Thursday sought to end a bitter row between the fiercely independent central bank and Chancellor Helmut Kohl's beleaguered coalition over tapping Bundesbank reserves in its bid to qualify for Europe's single currency.

Waigel stunned financial markets last month when he announced that the government was planning to seek a change in the law regulating the Bundesbank that would have allowed it to revalue the central bank's gold and currency reserves, which are priced well below market value.

The move would have caused the Bundesbank to transfer billions in realised profits to the federal government, aiding Bonn in its efforts to cap mounting budget deficits, pay off debt and come closer to meeting the fiscal targets outlined in the Maastricht treaty on European monetary union (EMU).

But it immediately backfired. Bundesbank council members came out in full force denouncing the grab for central bank gold as an outright attack on the bank's near sacrosanct independence and a damaging precedent for monetary union.

Germany, which had chastised other countries in Europe for resorting to "creative accounting" to make the grade for EMU, was suddenly suspected of resorting to hectic last-ditch efforts to put its own house in order.
Facing a storm of protest, Waigel quickly retreated, but even Bundesbank officials have acknowleged that the affair has probably done lasting damage to the central bank's image abroad.
